detail: The climactic slaying of Vapuṣmat and the flesh-and-blood śrāddha — the file's central, most load-bearing scene — is attributed to '(*Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* CXXXVI)' explicitly 'in Pargiter's numbering' (line 66, and Sources line 96 'CXXXIII–CXXXVI ... the slaying of Vapuṣmat with the offering of his flesh and blood'). But Pargiter's translation follows the Calcutta / Bibliotheca Indica recension, which 'ends abruptly in chapter 136, leaving the narrative of Dama halfway' (confirmed on en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markandeya_Purana). The completed vengeance and blood-libation appear only in the Bombay/Poona recension, concluding in chapter 137. So the blood-śrāddha is NOT in the edition it is cited to. Fix: attribute the climax to the fuller Bombay/Poona recension (ch. 137), and note that Pargiter's text — the very translation linked in the Sources — breaks off before it, rather than pinning it to 'Pargiter CXXXVI'.

Line 43 mislabels the date frames for Śaṅkara: "the ācārya's traditional floruit (scriptural/hagiographic 788–820 CE; [scholarly] c. 700 CE)". This presents 788–820 CE as the SCRIPTURAL/HAGIOGRAPHIC clock, but the corpus's own canonical node (07-acharyas-and-sampradayas/adi-shankara.md, line 41) states 788–820 CE is "an older, now-superseded convention" of *scholarly* dating — NOT a scriptural/traditional date. The genuine traditional/hagiographic clock per that node (line 4, 43) is the matha/Kāñcī tradition placing Śaṅkara in the 6th–5th c. BCE (born 509 BCE). Thus this file splits two ACADEMIC estimates (788–820 vs c.700 CE) across the two-clock frames and entirely omits the real scriptural/traditional (BCE) frame. Fix: relabel to '[scholarly] c. 700 CE (older superseded convention 788–820 CE)' and, if a scriptural frame is cited, give the traditional matha dating (c. 509 BCE / 6th–5th c. BCE) as adi-shankara.md does — keep the two clocks distinct per §4.

The file's central etiology misrepresents the content of its own cited source, Śiva Purāṇa, Kotirudra-saṃhitā ch. 13 (the pointer is correct — that chapter IS titled 'The origin of Vaṭuka' — but the story attributed to it is not what the chapter contains). The file (breadcrumb line 3 'Primary etiology'; §'The Kotirudra etiology' lines 22-24; disambiguation line 35) says Śiva 'brings forth a youthful manifestation of himself... not born of a womb but manifested from Śiva's own being... reckoned a son-form (putra-rūpa)' and that 'Vaṭuka, though called a son, IS Śiva himself in reduced, juvenile shape... not a separate deity.' The actual Kotirudra ch. 13 (Motilal/wisdomlib translation) narrates the FOUR Vaṭukas as the four SONS OF THE BRAHMIN SUDARŚANA and his wife Dukūlā, whom Śiva consecrates/establishes in the four quarters — 'because they had been established by Śiva and Śivā they are known as Vaṭukas.' They are born of a womb, are distinct persons consecrated by Śiva (not emanations of his being), and are four, not one. The file's 'non-dual son-who-is-the-father / emanated-from-Śiva's-own-being' reading is fabricated and directly contradicts the text; the singular 'the boy' framing throughout also conflicts with the text's four directional Vaṭukas (which additionally undercuts line 14's 'standalone youthful emanation'). Fix: rewrite the Kotirudra etiology to the Sudarśana/four-sons-consecrated-in-the-four-quarters story, or explicitly separate the Purāṇic four-Vaṭukas account from the later Tantric single boy-Bhairava persona rather than claiming the Purāṇa as the origin of the latter.

The file repeatedly states, as sourced fact from the Devī-Bhāgavata Purāṇa Book VI, that the foster-father who finds and adopts the mare-born Ekavīra is the childless king ŚATAJIT. §0 bullet 2: 'The DBP (Book VI) keeps the childless king **Śatajit** as the father-of-record...'; §1 final bullet: 'The **childless Yādava king Śatajit**, coming to the river, discovers the abandoned divine child... naming him **Ekavīra**. (*Devī-Bhāgavata Purāṇa* VI)'. This is a misattribution. The actual DBP text (Skandha VI, ch. 19 'On the origin of Haihayas from a mare' and ch. 20 'On the son born of mare by Hari', trans. Vijñānānanda on Wisdomlib) names the childless king as **TURVASU, the son of Yayāti, alias Harivarman** — 'The King Turvasu, the son of Yayāti... became exceedingly gladdened... [and] named the child Ekavīra.' The Studies-in-the-Upapurāṇas summary (the file's own cited source) confirms: 'Ekavira, who was given to Yayati's son Turvasu (alias Harivarman) by Visnu.' Śatajit appears nowhere in the DBP account; he belongs only to the mainstream Viṣṇu/Bhāgavata genealogy (Yadu → Sahasrajit → Śatajit → Haihaya) that the file quotes in §0 bullet 1. The author appears to have silently welded the DBP foundling onto the Viṣṇu-Purāṇa name to make the two genealogies agree. Fix: replace 'Śatajit' with 'Turvasu (son of Yayāti), alias Harivarman' in the DBP-attributed passages, and note that the DBP actually grafts Ekavīra onto Turvasu's line — a DIFFERENT branch from Yadu — which is itself the genealogical seam, not the smooth Śatajit continuity the file asserts.

Line 48 presents a direct quotation attributed to Devī-Bhāgavata VI.13: 'for full ten thousand years… out of anger, with their nails and beaks, like two maddened lions.' Verified against the cited source (Vijñānānanda tr., wisdomlib doc57238, the same translation the file cites): the text says only that the birds 'passed many years there' — it gives NO figure of 'ten thousand years' and contains NO 'maddened lions' comparison (it likens them only to blood-smeared Kiṃśuka trees). Both the number and the lion simile inside the quotation marks appear fabricated. Fix: replace the invented quote with the actual 'passed many years' wording, or drop the quotation marks and the specific figure. This error propagates to line 61 ('ten-thousand-year animal war'), line 70 ('duration (ten thousand years)'), and the Sources entry at line 100 ('ten thousand years of combat like two maddened lions') — all must be corrected.

Line 49 builds a duration 'variant' by attributing the phrase 'passed many years' to the MĀRKAṆḌEYA Purāṇa ('the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa says only that they "passed many years" so locked... the round ten-thousand-year span is the Devī-Bhāgavata's'). This is inverted: the phrase 'passed many years' actually occurs in the DEVĪ-BHĀGAVATA VI.13 (doc57238), while the Mārkaṇḍeya IX text (doc117037) gives no battle-duration phrase at all (its only 'years' reference is Vasiṣṭha's 'twelve years' by the Ganges). So the entire 'ten thousand (Devī-Bhāgavata) vs many years (Mārkaṇḍeya)' contrast is manufactured — in reality the Devī-Bhāgavata is the vague-'many years' text and neither source says 'ten thousand'. Fix: delete the false variant contrast; correctly attribute 'passed many years' to the Devī-Bhāgavata.

§I bullet 'The land and its holders' and the Sources line attribute the Gandharva king's name and troop count to Vālmīki: 'Their king is the Gandharva **Śailūṣa (Shailusha)**, and his host numbers **three crores** (thirty million) — often given as "the three crore sons of Śailūṣa" ... (Vālmīki *Uttara* 100).' This is a MISATTRIBUTION. The name Śailūṣa and the 'three crores of sons' figure come from the **Agni Purāṇa, ch. 11** (which summarizes: 'Bharata killed the wicked Gandharva named Śailūṣa and his three crores of sons who lived on the banks of the Sindhu'), NOT from Vālmīki's Uttara-kāṇḍa. In Vālmīki (Shastri translation, the very edition the file cites), Uttara sarga 100 does NOT name the Gandharva king, and sarga 101 says 'three hundred thousand' (three lakh) Gandharvas were slain — not three crore. The Agni Purāṇa is never cited anywhere in the file. Fix: attribute Śailūṣa + the three-crore figure to the Agni Purāṇa (ch. 11) with a distinct citation/tag, and note that Vālmīki's own count is three hundred thousand; do not present these as Vālmīki Uttara 100 material.

The 'deliberate two-country framing' is stated as settled Vālmīki fact but is not supported by the text. §III: 'Takṣaśilā... In the **Gandhāra country**' vs 'Puṣkalāvatī... In the (adjacent) **Gandharva country** — the land west of the region seated on Takṣaśilā'; and §VI: 'Vālmīki seats **Takṣaśilā in the Gāndhāra country** and **Puṣkalāvatī in the Gandharva country**; retellings that flatten "Gandharva" and "Gāndhāra" into one region lose the (probably deliberate) two-country framing.' But the Shastri Vālmīki (Uttara 101) places BOTH cities in one region: 'Bharata established Taksha in Takshashila and Pushkala in Pushkalavata, **in the country of the Gandharvas, in the ravishing region of Gandhara**.' The text treats Gandharva-country and Gāndhāra as the same place. Worse, where a two-word reading does appear in other translations the assignment is the REVERSE of the file's (Takshashila→land of the Gandharvas, Pushkalavati→land of Gāndhāra). So the file invents a distinction, fixes it in one (possibly backwards) direction, and then weaponizes it against 'retellings that flatten' the two. Fix: drop the settled 'two-country framing' claim (or tag it [disputed] and note translations vary and even reverse the assignment); state plainly that Vālmīki places both cities in the single Gandharva/Gāndhāra region.

The monograph "Of Death and Birth: Icakkiyamman, a Tamil Goddess, in Ritual and Story" is repeatedly attributed to "Perundevi Srinivasan" (lines 12, 14, 19, 54, 61, and the Sources entry line 90: "Perundevi Srinivasan, *Of Death and Birth: Icakkiyamman, a Tamil Goddess, in Ritual and Story*"). This is a misattribution. That book — full title "Of Death and Birth: Icakkiyamman, a Tamil Goddess, in Ritual and Story with a Film on DVD by the Author" (Ethno-Indology series, Harrassowitz Verlag, 2009, xvi+501 pp.) — was written by Barbara Schuler, not Perundevi Srinivasan. Perundevi Srinivasan is a real Tamil-goddess scholar (Siena University; her work centers on Mariyamman), but she did not author this title. Fix: change the author to "Barbara Schuler" everywhere the title appears, or drop the name and cite the title alone. Since this is the single most-cited scholarly source anchoring the article's Icakki material, the wrong author byline undermines every claim tagged to it.

The golden mark's location is misattributed to Ganguli. Line 46 says the reborn Jantu was 'distinguished by the golden mark on his left side'; line 66 doubles down: 'the exact locus of the golden mark (left side) are given in Ganguli'; line 40 says 'golden mark on his side where the fire touched him.' Ganguli's actual text (Vana Parva CXXVII–CXXVIII, sacred-texts m03127/m03128, mirrored on vyasaonline and wisdomlib) reads 'On his back there was that mark of gold' — the mark is on the BACK, not the left side. Fix: change 'left side' to 'back' in all three places, and drop the false 'given in Ganguli' certainty about the side.

The mother's name 'Kausalyā' is fabricated and falsely attributed to Ganguli. Line 46: 'to his original mother (Kausalyā in Ganguli's text)'; line 66: 'The mother's name (Kausalyā) ... are given in Ganguli.' In Ganguli's translation (and the CE) the mother is never named — she is referred to only collectively ('the mothers'/'those lovely women'). No Kausalyā appears in this episode. Fix: remove the name attribution; state that the mother is unnamed in the text.

Line 11 says the Mātali tale follows "Kṛṣṇa's own tale of [Dambhodbhava and the Nara-Nārāyaṇa]". The Dambhodbhava-upākhyāna is NOT narrated by Kṛṣṇa — it is narrated by Paraśurāma (Rāma Jāmadagnya). This is confirmed by the epic (Udyoga/Bhagavadyāna: Paraśurāma tells Dambhodbhava, Kaṇva tells Mātali, Nārada tells Gālava) and directly contradicted by the corpus's own canonical file 04-deep-dives/dambhodbhava-nara-narayana.md, whose breadcrumb reads 'narrated by Paraśurāma inside the Mahābhārata war-frame' and 'Rāma Jāmadagnya (Paraśurāma) speaks first among them.' Fix: change 'Kṛṣṇa's own tale of Dambhodbhava' to 'Paraśurāma's tale of Dambhodbhava.'

The file states three times that its chapter numbers follow the Ganguli/Calcutta vulgate (line 6: "Chapter numbers below follow the Ganguli/Calcutta vulgate, which the Critical Edition (BORI) renumbers"; line 51: "treat the figures above as vulgate references"; line 65 Sources: "Ganguli/Calcutta vulgate numbering: Jāpaka-upākhyāna (XII.189–193), Cirakārin-upākhyāna (XII.258), Kuṇḍadhara-upākhyāna (XII.263)"). But three of these are actually the BORI Critical-Edition numbers, not the vulgate. Verified against sacred-texts.com (Ganguli): the Cirakārī story is Ganguli Śānti Parva Section CCLXVI = 266 (m12b093.htm), not 258; the Jāpaka reciter-of-Gāyatrī material begins at Section CXCVII = 197 (m12b024.htm), not 189–193; Kuṇḍadhara likewise sits near CCLXX–CCLXXI (~270), not 263. Each cited number is ~8 lower than the true Ganguli figure — i.e. the file has given the Critical-Edition numbering and mislabeled it as the vulgate, exactly inverting its own claim. (The one genuinely-Ganguli figure is Pūjanī §CXXXVII/137, line 66, which is correct.) Fix: either relabel 189–193 / 258 / 263 as BORI Critical-Edition numbers, or replace them with the true Ganguli vulgate numbers (Jāpaka ~197–200, Cirakārī 266, Kuṇḍadhara ~271).

The 'Summā iru' line is attributed to Kandar Anubhūti verse 4 in two places: line 25 ('memorialised in the fourth verse of the Kandar Anubhuti — "Summā iru, col aṟa"... (Source: Kandar Anubhuti, v. 4)') and the Sources foot line 78 ('51 verses; esp. v. 4 ("Summā iru col aṟa…")'). The verse number is wrong. Line 10 in-page anchor link `[Lokanārkāvu](#the-thacholi-cycle-othenan-of-thacholi-manikkoth)` does not resolve. Line 54 and Sources line 97 attribute the 'ṣoḍaśa-rājakīya ("sixteen kings" eulogy)' listing Marutta among the sixteen greatest sovereigns to the '**Anuśāsana** Parva'. The classic Śoḍaśarājika passage naming Marutta is the Nārada-to-Sṛñjaya consolation narrative in the **Drona Parva** (Mahābhārata 7.55–71), echoed in the Śānti Parva — not the Anuśāsana Parva. Fix: cite Drona Parva (or Śānti Parva) for the sixteen-kings eulogy; keep Ashvamedhika Parva for the gold and the Saṃvarta episode (those are correct).

The file twice states the ending as settled, fully-preserved tradition: 'The tradition preserves the whole descent without softening the ending' (line 6) and 'the tradition records the blood-śrāddha exactly, with attribution' (line 76). This overstates certainty: the ending is recension-dependent — the most widely translated recension (Pargiter/Calcutta) actually breaks off (ch.136) before the blood-śrāddha, which survives only in the Bombay/Poona recension (ch.137). Fix: note the recension split rather than presenting the transmitted ending as uniform across the tradition.

Line 36 cites the Raktabīja motif to the wrong sub-cycle of the Devī Māhātmya: "(*Kedāra Vijaya*; cf. *Devī Māhātmya*, Mahiṣa-vadha cycle)". Raktabīja is not part of the Mahiṣa-vadha (second caritra, Mahishasura-slaying) episode; he appears in the third caritra, the Śumbha–Niśumbha cycle, where he is slain via Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā drinking his blood. Fix: change "Mahiṣa-vadha cycle" to "Śumbha–Niśumbha cycle" (or simply drop the sub-cycle label). Note the Sources entry (line 84) attributes the Raktabīja motif to the Devī Māhātmya correctly and without a wrong cycle name, so this is an internal inconsistency as well.

Line 20 states 'The Kotirudra-saṃhitā... is the fifth saṃhitā of the Śiva Purāṇa.' It is the FOURTH. The seven saṃhitās in order are Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa, Vāyavīya (confirmed Wikipedia/standard editions). Fix: change 'fifth' to 'fourth' (Umā is the fifth).

Following from the foster-father error: §1's phrase 'The **childless Yādava king Śatajit**' mislabels the adopter as a Yādava. In the DBP the adopter is Turvasu, who is Yadu's BROTHER (both sons of Yayāti), not a descendant of Yadu — Turvasu is the eponym of a separate line, not a Yādava. So even the ethnonym is wrong for the DBP's actual figure. Fix along with the name correction: the DBP adopter is a son of Yayāti (Turvasu/Harivarman), not a Yādava.

Line 5 (intro) says the Candravaṃśa ancestor "bears children by the Moon's grandson." Budha is the Moon's SON, not grandson — the file itself states this correctly at line 48 ("Budha (the planet Mercury), son of Soma/Candra by Tārā") and at line 49 makes Purūravas the Moon's grandson (Soma → Budha → Purūravas). As written, line 5 mislabels Budha and internally contradicts §4. Fix: "bears children by the Moon's son (Budha)" — or, if meaning the offspring, "mothers the Moon's grandson (Purūravas)."

§6 misrepresents the Rāmāyaṇa's own content. The file frames the churning-birth of Mithi as belonging to "the Purāṇic account" (VP IV.5; BhP IX.13.13) and then states: "The Rāmāyaṇa's Uttara-kāṇḍa telling centres on the curse, the pot-rebirth, and the blink; the bare dynastic succession Nimi → Mithi → Janaka is given elsewhere in the epic, in Janaka's own recitation of his lineage ... (Bāla-kāṇḍa sarga 71)." This is false: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Uttara-kāṇḍa sarga 57 — the very sarga the file repeatedly cites for the blink and pot-birth — itself narrates Mithi's birth from the churned/agitated body (araṇi) and names him "the King of Videha" and "the ancient Janaka," the origin of the race of Mithilā (confirmed via the Shastri translation, wisdomlib doc424828). Fix: correct §6 to state that the Uttara-kāṇḍa (sarga 57) also carries the churning-birth of Mithi and the Nimi→Mithi→Janaka succession, and reframe the churning-etymology as a shared Rāmāyaṇa-and-Purāṇic element rather than a Purāṇic-only elaboration given by Vālmīki merely 'elsewhere.'

Line 62 files the Bhāgavata under "The nagna-bhikṣā / chastity-test version" and cites "(Bhāgavata 4.1.15–33; … Padma Purāṇa)" as a source for the naked-alms-and-crying-infants chastity test provoked by Nārada/the three goddesses. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.1.15–33 does NOT contain that episode: it is the plain austerity-boon version — Atri performs tapas on Ṛkṣa mountain, the Trimūrti appear pleased and grant that portions of themselves (Soma, Dattātreya, Durvāsā) will be born as his sons — with no vow-breaking, no nagna demand, and no gods turned into infants. The file even contradicts itself: Sources line 90 correctly describes Bhāgavata 4.1.15–33 as only "the boon and the births of Soma, Dattātreya, Durvāsā." Fix: drop the Bhāgavata from the chastity-test attribution (leaving Padma Purāṇa and the sthala-māhātmyas, which do carry the nagna-bhikṣā/infants form), or explicitly note that the Bhāgavata gives only the austerity-boon variant, not the chastity test.

The granular per-episode chapter numbers in the second half of the cycle contradict the AITM/Deshpande edition the file itself cites (wisdomlib 'AITM translation portal', listed in Sources). File says the storming and Huṇḍa's death are at 'Padma Purāṇa, Bhūmi-khaṇḍa 117–119' (line 41) and the wedding at 'Bhūmi-khaṇḍa 119–120' (line 42). In that AITM edition, chapter 115 = 'Huṇḍa is Killed in the Battle', chapter 116 = 'Nahuṣa Marries Aśokasundarī', chapter 117 = 'Nahuṣa's Consecration' (https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-padma-purana/d/doc365209.html). So the file's numbers run ~3 chapters high relative to its own cited edition (Huṇḍa slain 115 not 117–119; wedding 116 not 119–120). The file does hedge 'chapters ~102–121' and 'Chapter boundaries vary by edition', which mitigates this, but the monotonic chapter-by-chapter map (102–103, 103–104, 104–106 … 117–119, 119–120) reads as precise attribution that does not match the source. Fix: align the back-half numbers to the AITM edition (Huṇḍa's death ~115, marriage ~116) or drop the per-episode chapter figures in favor of the hedged range.

Line 25 cross-ref links "[Chāndogya Upaniṣad](../../90-literature-corpus/smriti-itihasa-epics.md) 4.1–3" — but smriti-itihasa-epics.md is titled "Smṛti — Itihāsa (The Epics)" and covers only the Rāmāyaṇa/Mahābhārata; it does not treat the Chāndogya at all (grep finds no mention). Line 14 asserts a genuinely disputed genealogical point as settled and does so with an internal contradiction. It states Śukra's mother is 'a third, distinct figure (Pauloma/Divyā in some lists)' and then commands: 'Do not identify the beheaded wife with Pulomā (Cyavana's mother)... the texts keep her separate. [disputed]'. But (a) mainstream tradition (Mahābhārata Ādi-parva; Purāṇic Encyclopaedia; wisdomlib) repeatedly makes BOTH Cyavana and Śukra sons of Bhṛgu by Pulomā/Paulomī, so 'the texts keep her separate' overstates certainty — many texts in fact merge them; and (b) the passage names her 'Pauloma' while in the same breath forbidding identification with 'Pulomā' — Pauloma and Pulomā are the same name (patronymic vs. the wife herself), making the directive self-undermining. Fix: soften to a cataloged variant, e.g. '*Variant (genealogy):* some lists make Śukra's mother the same Pulomā who bore Cyavana; others treat her as a distinct wife designated only as Kāvyamātā' rather than issuing a firm 'do not identify / the texts keep her separate' instruction, and drop the confusing 'Pauloma' label from the 'distinct figure' clause. Famine length is misrepresented as a recensional dispute. Line 36 says 'a twelve-year famine in the telling (a fifteen-year span in some recensions)' with tag '[disputed — famine-length varies by recension]', and line 38 says 'throughout the twelve famine-years'; line 82 repeats 'the twelve- (var. fifteen-) year famine'. But the text the file itself cites (Devī-Bhāgavata XII, Vijñānānanda trans. — sacred-texts bk12ch09 / redzambala book-12-ch-9) gives BOTH numbers in the SAME chapter with different referents: 'Indra did not rain on this earth for fifteen years' (the drought), and 'the Muni Gautama fed and nourished for twelve years all the Munis' (the feeding period). So it is not a 12-vs-15 recensional variant of famine length; it is a 15-year drought plus a 12-year feeding in one text, and the file has inverted the source's actual famine figure (15) into a mere 'some recensions' variant. Fix: state the fifteen-year drought and the twelve-year feeding as the text's own two figures, and drop the '[disputed — varies by recension]' tag unless an actual variant recension is cited.
